title: Ruth Lyons: TV Pioneer
summary: Josh and Chuck profile Ruth Lyons (born Ruth Reeves, 1905, Cincinnati), an unsung pioneer of daytime TV talk shows. The episode covers her childhood and short time at the University of Cincinnati, her start at WKRC radio in 1929 after filling in on The Woman's Hour, her 1937 flood coverage, the Morning Matinee and Fifty Club, her move to TV in 1949, her national NBC offer that she declined to stay in Cincinnati, her ratings dominance, the color TV era, her Arthur Lee Simpkins dance controversy in 1952, her union solidarity, family tragedies including her daughter Candy's death in 1966, her 1967 retirement, and her later Save the Terminal role. The episode also discusses the Joe Franklin talk show claim and a listener correction about the NSA at Sugar Grove and the National Radio Quiet Zone.

segments.title: Opening and introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce Ruth Lyons as an unsung pioneer of television, claiming she invented the TV talk show format before Joe Franklin, and briefly discuss her character.

segments.title: Early life and first marriage
segments.summary: Ruth Reeves was born in Cincinnati in 1905 to a middle-class family; her grandmother was in the WCTU and she never drank. She dropped out of the University of Cincinnati after one year when her father fell ill, then worked at Willis Music Company and wrote songs, including the 1946 Christmas song Let's Light the Christmas Tree. She married Johnny Lyons, who was later transferred to Cleveland, and the marriage ended after about seven years.

segments.title: Start at WKRC radio
segments.summary: In 1929 Ruth got a full-time job at WKRC in Cincinnati and ad-libbed when filling in for the host of The Woman's Hour, which cost the regular host her job. She went on to host several shows, and the station was later part of her early radio career.

segments.title: 1937 flood and promotion to program director
segments.summary: Ruth stayed on the air for about forty-eight hours during the 1937 Cincinnati flood, reading bulletins on relief, and was subsequently promoted to program director.

segments.title: Morning Matinee and Christmas Fund
segments.summary: Ruth moved to Crosley Broadcasting's station in 1942 and built the Morning Matinee, which featured product testing by women, music, and games. She started the Christmas Fund in 1939 at Cincinnati Children's Hospital, which raised about a thousand dollars in its first year and fifty-four thousand by 1943.

segments.title: Second marriage, daughter Candy, and the Fifty Club
segments.summary: Ruth married Herman Newman, a semantics professor, and had a daughter, Candy, in 1944 after a stillbirth. The Fifty Club was a luncheon and radio show at the Gibson Hotel that grew so popular it had to move to a larger venue.

segments.title: Move to television and national offer
segments.summary: In 1949 the Fifty Club moved to TV. Ruth struggled with studio lights and engineers. NBC offered a national show in 1951, but she declined to move to New York and stayed in the Crosley market, where her show was the highest-rated daytime program in the country from 1952 to 1964. Her show reached about seven million viewers and was carried on radio too.

segments.title: Color TV, set design, and format
segments.summary: The show was among the first in the region to air in color in 1957, making Cincinnati known as Colortown USA. Ruth staged a makeup contest with the audience. The set looked like a living room, and her interview seat was a rocker-love seat. She kept her microphone inside a bouquet of flowers. Guests included Sammy Davis Jr., Duke Ellington, Bob Hope, and Peter, Paul and Mary.

segments.title: Memoir and on-air advertising style
segments.summary: Josh recommends her memoir Remember with Me (1969). Ruth ad-libbed sponsor copy and sometimes teased sponsors, and she refused endorsements she did not believe in. A canned broccoli sponsor reportedly rose from number seven to number one.

segments.title: Integrated advertising and critics
segments.summary: Ruth's housekeeping segments and ironing contest promoted sponsors; the hosts compare this to integrated advertising. A 1960 Ladies Home Journal profile criticized her, and the hosts argue the criticism was coded.

segments.title: Arthur Lee Simpkins dance and labor solidarity
segments.summary: In 1952 Ruth danced on air with Black singer Arthur Lee Simpkins to calm his nerves, causing controversy; she defended it on the next day's show. She also supported the striking musicians' union and staff, including Elsa Sewele, who ran her show.

segments.title: Family tragedy, retirement, and death
segments.summary: Ruth's sister Rose died in 1964 after cancer, and Ruth had a minor stroke. Candy was diagnosed with breast cancer and died in 1966 at twenty-one. Ruth retired in 1967, announced by the station's vice president. She later served as honorary chairman of the 1972 Save the Terminal campaign and died in 1988 at eighty-one.

segments.title: 1957 All-Star ballot stuffing
segments.summary: Ruth led a drive to stuff the ballot box for Cincinnati Reds players in the 1957 All-Star Game, which the hosts discuss as a footnote.

segments.title: Listener mail: National Radio Quiet Zone correction
segments.summary: Listener Stephen Cursey, author of The Quiet Zone, writes that the NSA remains active at Sugar Grove and that the government retained the classified antennas there after the Navy's operations and housing were partly sold.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off and direct listeners to iHeartRadio for more podcasts.
